Solving Fermat: Andrew Wiles

Andrew Wiles devoted much of his entire career to proving Fermat's Last Theorem, the world's most famous mathematical problem. In 1993, he made front-page headlines when he announced a proof of the problem, but this was not the end of the story; an error in his calculation jeopardized his life's work. Andrew Wiles spoke to NOVA and described how he came to terms with the mistake, and eventually went on to achieve his life's ambition.

NOVA: Many great scientific discoveries are the result of obsession, but in your case that obsession has held you since you were a child.

ANDREW WILES: I grew up in Cambridge in England, and my love of mathematics dates from those early childhood days. I loved doing problems in school. I'd take them home and make up new ones of my own. But the best problem I ever found, I found in my local public library. I was just browsing through the section of math books and I found this one book, which was all about one particular problem—Fermat's Last Theorem. This problem had been unsolved by mathematicians for 300 years. It looked so simple, and yet all the great mathematicians in history couldn't solve it. Here was a problem, that I, a ten year old, could understand and I knew from that moment that I would never let it go. I had to solve it.

NOVA: Who was Fermat and what was his Last Theorem?

AW: Fermat was a 17th-century mathematician who wrote a note in the margin of his book stating a particular proposition and claiming to have proved it. His proposition was about an equation which is closely related to Pythagoras' equation. Pythagoras' equation gives you:
x2 + y2 = z2

You can ask, what are the whole number solutions to this equation, and you can see that:

32 + 42 = 52

and

52 + 122 = 132

And if you go on looking then you find more and more such solutions. Fermat then considered the cubed version of this equation:

x3 + y3 = z3

He raised the question: can you find solutions to the cubed equation? He claimed that there were none. In fact, he claimed that for the general family of equations:

xn + yn = zn where n is bigger than 2

it is impossible to find a solution. That's Fermat's Last Theorem.

NOVA: So Fermat said because he could not find any solutions to this equation, then there were no solutions?

AW: He did more than that. Just because we can't find a solution it doesn't mean that there isn't one. Mathematicians aren't satisfied because they know there are no solutions up to four million or four billion, they really want to know that there are no solutions up to infinity. And to do that we need a proof. Fermat said he had a proof. Unfortunately, all he ever wrote down was: "I have a truly marvelous demonstration of this proposition which this margin is too narrow to contain."

NOVA: What do you mean by a proof?

AW: In a mathematical proof you have a line of reasoning consisting of many, many steps, that are almost self-evident. If the proof we write down is really rigorous, then nobody can ever prove it wrong. There are proofs that date back to the Greeks that are still valid today.

NOVA: So the challenge was to rediscover Fermat's proof of the Last Theorem. Why did it become so famous?

AW: Well, some mathematics problems look simple, and you try them for a year or so, and then you try them for a hundred years, and it turns out that they're extremely hard to solve. There's no reason why these problems shouldn't be easy, and yet they turn out to be extremely intricate. The Last Theorem is the most beautiful example of this.

NOVA: But finding a proof has no applications in the real world; it is a purely abstract question. So why have people put so much effort into finding a proof?

AW: Pure mathematicians just love to try unsolved problems—they love a challenge. And as time passed and no proof was found, it became a real challenge. I've read letters in the early 19th century which said that it was an embarrassment to mathematics that the Last Theorem had not been solved. And of course, it's very special because Fermat said that he had a proof.

NOVA: How did you begin looking for the proof?

AW: In my early teens I tried to tackle the problem as I thought Fermat might have tried it. I reckoned that he wouldn't have known much more math than I knew as a teenager. Then when I reached college, I realized that many people had thought about the problem during the 18th and 19th centuries and so I studied those methods. But I still wasn't getting anywhere. Then when I became a researcher, I decided that I should put the problem aside. It's not that I forgot about it—it was always there—but I realized that the only techniques we had to tackle it had been around for 130 years. It didn't seem that these techniques were really getting to the root of the problem. The problem with working on Fermat was that you could spend years getting nowhere. It's fine to work on any problem, so long as it generates interesting mathematics along the way—even if you don't solve it at the end of the day. The definition of a good mathematical problem is the mathematics it generates rather than the problem itself.

NOVA: It seems that the Last Theorem was considered impossible, and that mathematicians could not risk wasting getting nowhere. But then in 1986 everything changed. A breakthrough by Ken Ribet at the University of California at Berkeley linked Fermat's Last Theorem to another unsolved problem, the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. Can you remember how you reacted to this news?

AW: It was one evening at the end of the summer of 1986 when I was sipping iced tea at the house of a friend. Casually in the middle of a conversation this friend told me that Ken Ribet had proved a link between Taniyama-Shimura and Fermat's Last Theorem. I was electrified. I knew that moment that the course of my life was changing because this meant that to prove Fermat's Last Theorem all I had to do was to prove the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. It meant that my childhood dream was now a respectable thing to work on. I just knew that I could never let that go.

NOVA: So, because Taniyama-Shimura was a modern problem, this meant that working on it, and by implication trying to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, was respectable.

AW: Yes. Nobody had any idea how to approach Taniyama-Shimura but at least it was mainstream mathematics. I could try and prove results, which, even if they didn't get the whole thing, would be worthwhile mathematics. So the romance of Fermat, which had held me all my life, was now combined with a problem that was professionally acceptable.

NOVA: At this point you decided to work in complete isolation. You told nobody that you were embarking on a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Why was that?

AW: I realized that anything to do with Fermat's Last Theorem generates too much interest. You can't really focus yourself for years unless you have undivided concentration, which too many spectators would have destroyed.

NOVA: But presumably you told your wife what you were doing?

AW: My wife's only known me while I've been working on Fermat. I told her on our honeymoon, just a few days after we got married. My wife had heard of Fermat's Last Theorem, but at that time she had no idea of the romantic significance it had for mathematicians, that it had been such a thorn in our flesh for so many years.

NOVA: On a day-to-day basis, how did you go about constructing your proof?

AW: I used to come up to my study, and start trying to find patterns. I tried doing calculations which explain some little piece of mathematics. I tried to fit it in with some previous broad conceptual understanding of some part of mathematics that would clarify the particular problem I was thinking about. Sometimes that would involve going and looking it up in a book to see how it's done there. Sometimes it was a question of modifying things a bit, doing a little extra calculation. And sometimes I realized that nothing that had ever been done before was any use at all. Then I just had to find something completely new; it's a mystery where that comes from. I carried this problem around in my head basically the whole time. I would wake up with it first thing in the morning, I would be thinking about it all day, and I would be thinking about it when I went to sleep. Without distraction, I would have the same thing going round and round in my mind. The only way I could relax was when I was with my children. Young children simply aren't interested in Fermat. They just want to hear a story and they're not going to let you do anything else.

NOVA: Usually people work in groups and use each other for support. What did you do when you hit a brick wall?

AW: When I got stuck and I didn't know what to do next, I would go out for a walk. I'd often walk down by the lake. Walking has a very good effect in that you're in this state of relaxation, but at the same time you're allowing the sub-conscious to work on you. And often if you have one particular thing buzzing in your mind then you don't need anything to write with or any desk. I'd always have a pencil and paper ready and, if I really had an idea, I'd sit down at a bench and I'd start scribbling away.

NOVA: So for seven years you're pursuing this proof. Presumably there are periods of self-doubt mixed with the periods of success.

AW: Perhaps I can best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of a journey through a dark unexplored mansion. You enter the first room of the mansion and it's completely dark. You stumble around bumping into the furniture, but gradually you learn where each piece of furniture is. Finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch, you turn it on, and suddenly it's all illuminated. You can see exactly where you were. Then you move into the next room and spend another six months in the dark. So each of these breakthroughs, while sometimes they're momentary, sometimes over a period of a day or two, they are the culmination of—and couldn't exist without—the many months of stumbling around in the dark that proceed them.

NOVA: And during those seven years, you could never be sure of achieving a complete proof.

AW: I really believed that I was on the right track, but that did not mean that I would necessarily reach my goal. It could be that the methods needed to take the next step may simply be beyond present day mathematics. Perhaps the methods I needed to complete the proof would not be invented for a hundred years. So even if I was on the right track, I could be living in the wrong century.

NOVA: Then eventually in 1993, you made the crucial breakthrough.

AW: Yes, it was one morning in late May. My wife, Nada, was out with the children and I was sitting at my desk thinking about the last stage of the proof. I was casually looking at a research paper and there was one sentence that just caught my attention. It mentioned a 19th-century construction, and I suddenly realized that I should be able to use that to complete the proof. I went on into the afternoon and I forgot to go down for lunch, and by about three or four o'clock, I was really convinced that this would solve the last remaining problem. It got to about tea time and I went downstairs and Nada was very surprised that I'd arrived so late. Then I told her I'd solved Fermat's Last Theorem.

NOVA: The New York Times exclaimed "At Last Shout of 'Eureka!' in Age-Old Math Mystery," but unknown to them, and to you, there was an error in your proof. What was the error?

AW: It was an error in a crucial part of the argument, but it was something so subtle that I'd missed it completely until that point. The error is so abstract that it can't really be described in simple terms. Even explaining it to a mathematician would require the mathematician to spend two or three months studying that part of the manuscript in great detail.

NOVA: Eventually, after a year of work, and after inviting the Cambridge mathematician Richard Taylor to work with you on the error, you managed to repair the proof. The question that everybody asks is this; is your proof the same as Fermat's?

AW: There's no chance of that. Fermat couldn't possibly have had this proof. It's 150 pages long. It's a 20th-century proof. It couldn't have been done in the 19th century, let alone the 17th century. The techniques used in this proof just weren't around in Fermat's time.

NOVA: So Fermat's original proof is still out there somewhere.

AW: I don't believe Fermat had a proof. I think he fooled himself into thinking he had a proof. But what has made this problem special for amateurs is that there's a tiny possibility that there does exist an elegant 17th-century proof.

NOVA: So some mathematicians might continue to look for the original proof. What will you do next?

AW: There's no problem that will mean the same to me. Fermat was my childhood passion. There's nothing to replace it. I'll try other problems. I'm sure that some of them will be very hard and I'll have a sense of achievement again, but nothing will mean the same to me. There's no other problem in mathematics that could hold me the way that this one did. There is a sense of melancholy. We've lost something that's been with us for so long, and something that drew a lot of us into mathematics. But perhaps that's always the way with math problems, and we just have to find new ones to capture our attention. People have told me I've taken away their problem—can't I give them something else? I feel some sense of responsibility. I hope that seeing the excitement of solving this problem will make young mathematicians realize that there are lots and lots of other problems in mathematics which are going to be just as challenging in the future.

NOVA: What is the main challenge now?

AW: The greatest problem for mathematicians now is probably the Riemann Hypothesis. But it's not a problem that can be simply stated.

NOVA: And is there any one particular thought that remains with you now that Fermat's Last Theorem has been laid to rest?

AW: Certainly one thing that I've learned is that it is important to pick a problem based on how much you care about it. However impenetrable it seems, if you don't try it, then you can never do it. Always try the problem that matters most to you. I had this rare privilege of being able to pursue in my adult life, what had been my childhood dream. I know it's a rare privilege, but if one can really tackle something in adult life that means that much to you, then it's more rewarding than anything I can imagine.

NOVA: And now that journey is over, there must be a certain sadness?

AW: There is a certain sense of sadness, but at the same time there is this tremendous sense of achievement. There's also a sense of freedom. I was so obsessed by this problem that I was thinking about it all the time—when I woke up in the morning, when I went to sleep at night—and that went on for eight years. That's a long time to think about one thing. That particular odyssey is now over. My mind is now at rest. Andrew Wiles | Math's Hidden Woman | Pythagorean Puzzle

NOVA: So the challenge was to rediscover Fermat's proof of the Last Theorem. Why did it become so famous?

AW: Well, some mathematics problems look simple, and you try them for a year or so, and then you try them for a hundred years, and it turns out that they're extremely hard to solve. There's no reason why these problems shouldn't be easy, and yet they turn out to be extremely intricate. The Last Theorem is the most beautiful example of this.

NOVA: But finding a proof has no applications in the real world; it is a purely abstract question. So why have people put so much effort into finding a proof?

AW: Pure mathematicians just love to try unsolved problems—they love a challenge. And as time passed and no proof was found, it became a real challenge. I've read letters in the early 19th century which said that it was an embarrassment to mathematics that the Last Theorem had not been solved. And of course, it's very special because Fermat said that he had a proof.

NOVA: How did you begin looking for the proof?

AW: In my early teens I tried to tackle the problem as I thought Fermat might have tried it. I reckoned that he wouldn't have known much more math than I knew as a teenager. Then when I reached college, I realized that many people had thought about the problem during the 18th and 19th centuries and so I studied those methods. But I still wasn't getting anywhere. Then when I became a researcher, I decided that I should put the problem aside. It's not that I forgot about it—it was always there—but I realized that the only techniques we had to tackle it had been around for 130 years. It didn't seem that these techniques were really getting to the root of the problem. The problem with working on Fermat was that you could spend years getting nowhere. It's fine to work on any problem, so long as it generates interesting mathematics along the way—even if you don't solve it at the end of the day. The definition of a good mathematical problem is the mathematics it generates rather than the problem itself.

NOVA: It seems that the Last Theorem was considered impossible, and that mathematicians could not risk wasting getting nowhere. But then in 1986 everything changed. A breakthrough by Ken Ribet at the University of California at Berkeley linked Fermat's Last Theorem to another unsolved problem, the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. Can you remember how you reacted to this news?

AW: It was one evening at the end of the summer of 1986 when I was sipping iced tea at the house of a friend. Casually in the middle of a conversation this friend told me that Ken Ribet had proved a link between Taniyama-Shimura and Fermat's Last Theorem. I was electrified. I knew that moment that the course of my life was changing because this meant that to prove Fermat's Last Theorem all I had to do was to prove the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. It meant that my childhood dream was now a respectable thing to work on. I just knew that I could never let that go.

NOVA: So, because Taniyama-Shimura was a modern problem, this meant that working on it, and by implication trying to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, was respectable.

AW: Yes. Nobody had any idea how to approach Taniyama-Shimura but at least it was mainstream mathematics. I could try and prove results, which, even if they didn't get the whole thing, would be worthwhile mathematics. So the romance of Fermat, which had held me all my life, was now combined with a problem that was professionally acceptable.

NOVA: At this point you decided to work in complete isolation. You told nobody that you were embarking on a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Why was that?

AW: I realized that anything to do with Fermat's Last Theorem generates too much interest. You can't really focus yourself for years unless you have undivided concentration, which too many spectators would have destroyed.

NOVA: But presumably you told your wife what you were doing?

AW: My wife's only known me while I've been working on Fermat. I told her on our honeymoon, just a few days after we got married. My wife had heard of Fermat's Last Theorem, but at that time she had no idea of the romantic significance it had for mathematicians, that it had been such a thorn in our flesh for so many years.

NOVA: On a day-to-day basis, how did you go about constructing your proof?

AW: I used to come up to my study, and start trying to find patterns. I tried doing calculations which explain some little piece of mathematics. I tried to fit it in with some previous broad conceptual understanding of some part of mathematics that would clarify the particular problem I was thinking about. Sometimes that would involve going and looking it up in a book to see how it's done there. Sometimes it was a question of modifying things a bit, doing a little extra calculation. And sometimes I realized that nothing that had ever been done before was any use at all. Then I just had to find something completely new; it's a mystery where that comes from. I carried this problem around in my head basically the whole time. I would wake up with it first thing in the morning, I would be thinking about it all day, and I would be thinking about it when I went to sleep. Without distraction, I would have the same thing going round and round in my mind. The only way I could relax was when I was with my children. Young children simply aren't interested in Fermat. They just want to hear a story and they're not going to let you do anything else.

NOVA: Usually people work in groups and use each other for support. What did you do when you hit a brick wall?

AW: When I got stuck and I didn't know what to do next, I would go out for a walk. I'd often walk down by the lake. Walking has a very good effect in that you're in this state of relaxation, but at the same time you're allowing the sub-conscious to work on you. And often if you have one particular thing buzzing in your mind then you don't need anything to write with or any desk. I'd always have a pencil and paper ready and, if I really had an idea, I'd sit down at a bench and I'd start scribbling away.

NOVA: So for seven years you're pursuing this proof. Presumably there are periods of self-doubt mixed with the periods of success.

AW: Perhaps I can best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of a journey through a dark unexplored mansion. You enter the first room of the mansion and it's completely dark. You stumble around bumping into the furniture, but gradually you learn where each piece of furniture is. Finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch, you turn it on, and suddenly it's all illuminated. You can see exactly where you were. Then you move into the next room and spend another six months in the dark. So each of these breakthroughs, while sometimes they're momentary, sometimes over a period of a day or two, they are the culmination of—and couldn't exist without—the many months of stumbling around in the dark that proceed them.

NOVA: And during those seven years, you could never be sure of achieving a complete proof.

AW: I really believed that I was on the right track, but that did not mean that I would necessarily reach my goal. It could be that the methods needed to take the next step may simply be beyond present day mathematics. Perhaps the methods I needed to complete the proof would not be invented for a hundred years. So even if I was on the right track, I could be living in the wrong century.

NOVA: Then eventually in 1993, you made the crucial breakthrough.

AW: Yes, it was one morning in late May. My wife, Nada, was out with the children and I was sitting at my desk thinking about the last stage of the proof. I was casually looking at a research paper and there was one sentence that just caught my attention. It mentioned a 19th-century construction, and I suddenly realized that I should be able to use that to complete the proof. I went on into the afternoon and I forgot to go down for lunch, and by about three or four o'clock, I was really convinced that this would solve the last remaining problem. It got to about tea time and I went downstairs and Nada was very surprised that I'd arrived so late. Then I told her I'd solved Fermat's Last Theorem.

NOVA: The New York Times exclaimed "At Last Shout of 'Eureka!' in Age-Old Math Mystery," but unknown to them, and to you, there was an error in your proof. What was the error?

AW: It was an error in a crucial part of the argument, but it was something so subtle that I'd missed it completely until that point. The error is so abstract that it can't really be described in simple terms. Even explaining it to a mathematician would require the mathematician to spend two or three months studying that part of the manuscript in great detail.

NOVA: Eventually, after a year of work, and after inviting the Cambridge mathematician Richard Taylor to work with you on the error, you managed to repair the proof. The question that everybody asks is this; is your proof the same as Fermat's?

AW: There's no chance of that. Fermat couldn't possibly have had this proof. It's 150 pages long. It's a 20th-century proof. It couldn't have been done in the 19th century, let alone the 17th century. The techniques used in this proof just weren't around in Fermat's time.

NOVA: So Fermat's original proof is still out there somewhere.

AW: I don't believe Fermat had a proof. I think he fooled himself into thinking he had a proof. But what has made this problem special for amateurs is that there's a tiny possibility that there does exist an elegant 17th-century proof.

NOVA: So some mathematicians might continue to look for the original proof. What will you do next?

AW: There's no problem that will mean the same to me. Fermat was my childhood passion. There's nothing to replace it. I'll try other problems. I'm sure that some of them will be very hard and I'll have a sense of achievement again, but nothing will mean the same to me. There's no other problem in mathematics that could hold me the way that this one did. There is a sense of melancholy. We've lost something that's been with us for so long, and something that drew a lot of us into mathematics. But perhaps that's always the way with math problems, and we just have to find new ones to capture our attention. People have told me I've taken away their problem—can't I give them something else? I feel some sense of responsibility. I hope that seeing the excitement of solving this problem will make young mathematicians realize that there are lots and lots of other problems in mathematics which are going to be just as challenging in the future.

NOVA: What is the main challenge now?

AW: The greatest problem for mathematicians now is probably the Riemann Hypothesis. But it's not a problem that can be simply stated.

NOVA: And is there any one particular thought that remains with you now that Fermat's Last Theorem has been laid to rest?

AW: Certainly one thing that I've learned is that it is important to pick a problem based on how much you care about it. However impenetrable it seems, if you don't try it, then you can never do it. Always try the problem that matters most to you. I had this rare privilege of being able to pursue in my adult life, what had been my childhood dream. I know it's a rare privilege, but if one can really tackle something in adult life that means that much to you, then it's more rewarding than anything I can imagine.

NOVA: And now that journey is over, there must be a certain sadness?

AW: There is a certain sense of sadness, but at the same time there is this tremendous sense of achievement. There's also a sense of freedom. I was so obsessed by this problem that I was thinking about it all the time—when I woke up in the morning, when I went to sleep at night—and that went on for eight years. That's a long time to think about one thing. That particular odyssey is now over. My mind is now at rest. Andrew Wiles | Math's Hidden Woman | Pythagorean Puzzle

sentences.zh: AW：我意识到任何与费马大定理有关的事情都会引起太多的兴趣。

sentences.en: You can't really focus yourself for years unless you have undivided concentration, which too many spectators would have destroyed.
sentences.zh: 除非你全神贯注，否则你不可能多年真正集中注意力，而太多的观众会破坏你的注意力。

sentences.en: NOVA: But presumably you told your wife what you were doing?
sentences.zh: NOVA：但想必你告诉了你的妻子你在做什么？

sentences.en: AW: My wife's only known me while I've been working on Fermat.
sentences.zh: AW：我妻子是在我从事费马研究时才认识我的。

sentences.en: I told her on our honeymoon, just a few days after we got married.
sentences.zh: 我在蜜月时告诉她的，就在我们结婚几天后。

sentences.en: My wife had heard of Fermat's Last Theorem, but at that time she had no idea of the romantic significance it had for mathematicians, that it had been such a thorn in our flesh for so many years.
sentences.zh: 我的妻子听说过费马大定理，但当时她并不知道它对数学家的浪漫意义，多年来它一直是我们的肉中刺。

sentences.en: NOVA: On a day-to-day basis, how did you go about constructing your proof?
sentences.zh: NOVA：在日常工作中，你是如何构建你的证明的？

sentences.en: AW: I used to come up to my study, and start trying to find patterns.
sentences.zh: AW：我过去常常开始研究，并开始尝试寻找模式。

sentences.en: I tried doing calculations which explain some little piece of mathematics.
sentences.zh: 我尝试做一些计算来解释一些数学知识。

sentences.en: I tried to fit it in with some previous broad conceptual understanding of some part of mathematics that would clarify the particular problem I was thinking about.
sentences.zh: 我试图将其与之前对数学某些部分的一些广泛的概念性理解相结合，以澄清我正在考虑的特定问题。

sentences.en: Sometimes that would involve going and looking it up in a book to see how it's done there.
sentences.zh: 有时这需要去书本上查找，看看它是如何完成的。

sentences.en: Sometimes it was a question of modifying things a bit, doing a little extra calculation.
sentences.zh: 有时这是一个稍微修改一些东西，做一些额外计算的问题。

sentences.en: And sometimes I realized that nothing that had ever been done before was any use at all.
sentences.zh: 有时我意识到以前做过的任何事情都没有任何用处。

sentences.en: Then I just had to find something completely new; it's a mystery where that comes from.
sentences.zh: 然后我只需要找到一些全新的东西；它是从哪里来的还是个谜。

sentences.en: I carried this problem around in my head basically the whole time.
sentences.zh: 我基本上一直在脑子里萦绕着这个问题。

sentences.en: I would wake up with it first thing in the morning, I would be thinking about it all day, and I would be thinking about it when I went to sleep.
sentences.zh: 我早上醒来的第一件事就是想到它，我会整天想着它，当我睡觉时我也会想着它。

sentences.en: Without distraction, I would have the same thing going round and round in my mind.
sentences.zh: 如果没有分心，同样的事情就会在我的脑海里转来转去。

sentences.en: The only way I could relax was when I was with my children.
sentences.zh: 我唯一能放松的方式就是和孩子们在一起。

sentences.en: Young children simply aren't interested in Fermat.
sentences.zh: 小孩子对费马根本不感兴趣。

sentences.en: They just want to hear a story and they're not going to let you do anything else.
sentences.zh: 他们只是想听一个故事，不会让你做任何其他事情。

sentences.en: NOVA: Usually people work in groups and use each other for support.
sentences.zh: NOVA：通常人们会分组工作并互相支持。

sentences.en: What did you do when you hit a brick wall?
sentences.zh: 当你撞到砖墙时你会做什么？

sentences.en: AW: When I got stuck and I didn't know what to do next, I would go out for a walk.
sentences.zh: AW：当我遇到困难并且不知道下一步该做什么时，我会出去散步。

sentences.en: I'd often walk down by the lake.
sentences.zh: 我经常在湖边散步。

sentences.en: Walking has a very good effect in that you're in this state of relaxation, but at the same time you're allowing the sub-conscious to work on you.
sentences.zh: 散步有很好的效果，因为你可以处于这种放松的状态，但同时你也可以让潜意识对你起作用。

sentences.en: And often if you have one particular thing buzzing in your mind then you don't need anything to write with or any desk.
sentences.zh: 通常，如果您脑子里有一件特定的事情在嗡嗡作响，那么您就不需要任何可以用来写字的东西或任何桌子。

sentences.en: I'd always have a pencil and paper ready and, if I really had an idea, I'd sit down at a bench and I'd start scribbling away.
sentences.zh: 我总是准备好铅笔和纸，如果我真的有一个想法，我就会坐在长凳上，开始乱写乱画。

sentences.en: NOVA: So for seven years you're pursuing this proof.
sentences.zh: NOVA：所以七年来你一直在追求这个证明。

sentences.en: Presumably there are periods of self-doubt mixed with the periods of success.
sentences.zh: 想必在成功的时期中也夹杂着自我怀疑的时期。

sentences.en: AW: Perhaps I can best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of a journey through a dark unexplored mansion.
sentences.zh: AW：也许我最能描述我做数学的经历，就是穿越一座未经探索的黑暗宅邸的旅程。

sentences.en: You enter the first room of the mansion and it's completely dark.
sentences.zh: 你进入宅邸的第一个房间，里面一片漆黑。

sentences.en: You stumble around bumping into the furniture, but gradually you learn where each piece of furniture is.
sentences.zh: 你跌跌撞撞地撞到了家具，但渐渐地你就知道了每件家具的位置。

sentences.en: Finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch, you turn it on, and suddenly it's all illuminated.
sentences.zh: 最后，大约六个月后，你找到灯开关，打开它，突然间一切都亮了。

sentences.en: You can see exactly where you were.
sentences.zh: 您可以准确地看到您所在的位置。

sentences.en: Then you move into the next room and spend another six months in the dark.
sentences.zh: 然后你搬进隔壁房间，在黑暗中又度过了六个月。

sentences.en: So each of these breakthroughs, while sometimes they're momentary, sometimes over a period of a day or two, they are the culmination of—and couldn't exist without—the many months of stumbling around in the dark that proceed them.
sentences.zh: 因此，每一项突破虽然有时是短暂的，有时是一两天的时间，但它们都是数月在黑暗中摸索的结果，而且如果没有这些突破，它们就不可能存在。

sentences.en: NOVA: And during those seven years, you could never be sure of achieving a complete proof.
sentences.zh: NOVA：在那七年里，你永远无法确定能否获得完整的证明。

sentences.en: AW: I really believed that I was on the right track, but that did not mean that I would necessarily reach my goal.
sentences.zh: AW：我确实相信自己走在正确的道路上，但这并不意味着我一定会达到目标。

sentences.en: It could be that the methods needed to take the next step may simply be beyond present day mathematics.
sentences.zh: 采取下一步所需的方法可能根本超出了当今的数学范围。

sentences.en: Perhaps the methods I needed to complete the proof would not be invented for a hundred years.
sentences.zh: 也许我完成证明所需的方法一百年后都不会被发明出来。

sentences.en: So even if I was on the right track, I could be living in the wrong century.
sentences.zh: 因此，即使我走在正确的道路上，我也可能生活在错误的世纪。

sentences.en: NOVA: Then eventually in 1993, you made the crucial breakthrough.
sentences.zh: NOVA：最终在 1993 年，你取得了关键的突破。

sentences.en: AW: Yes, it was one morning in late May.
sentences.zh: AW：是的，那是五月下旬的一个早晨。

sentences.en: My wife, Nada, was out with the children and I was sitting at my desk thinking about the last stage of the proof.
sentences.zh: 我的妻子娜达（Nada）带着孩子们出去了，而我则坐在办公桌前思考证明的最后阶段。

sentences.en: I was casually looking at a research paper and there was one sentence that just caught my attention.
sentences.zh: 我随意地看一篇研究论文，有一句话引起了我的注意。

sentences.en: It mentioned a 19th-century construction, and I suddenly realized that I should be able to use that to complete the proof.
sentences.zh: 它提到了一个19世纪的构造，我突​​然意识到我应该可以用它来完成证明。

sentences.en: I went on into the afternoon and I forgot to go down for lunch, and by about three or four o'clock, I was really convinced that this would solve the last remaining problem.
sentences.zh: 一直持续到下午，我忘记了下去吃午饭，到了大约三四点的时候，我真的确信这将解决最后一个剩下的问题。

sentences.en: It got to about tea time and I went downstairs and Nada was very surprised that I'd arrived so late.
sentences.zh: 下午茶时间到了，我下了楼，纳达对我这么晚才到感到非常惊讶。

sentences.en: Then I told her I'd solved Fermat's Last Theorem.
sentences.zh: 然后我告诉她我已经解决了费马大定理。

sentences.en: NOVA: The New York Times exclaimed "At Last Shout of 'Eureka!'
sentences.zh: NOVA：《纽约时报》惊呼“‘尤里卡’的最后一声呐喊！”

sentences.en: in Age-Old Math Mystery," but unknown to them, and to you, there was an error in your proof.
sentences.zh: 在古老的数学之谜中”，但他们和你都不知道，你的证明中有一个错误。

sentences.en: What was the error?
sentences.zh: 错误是什么？

sentences.en: AW: It was an error in a crucial part of the argument, but it was something so subtle that I'd missed it completely until that point.
sentences.zh: AW：这是论证的关键部分中的一个错误，但它是如此微妙，以至于我在那之前完全错过了它。

sentences.en: The error is so abstract that it can't really be described in simple terms.
sentences.zh: 该错误非常抽象，无法用简单的术语来描述。

sentences.en: Even explaining it to a mathematician would require the mathematician to spend two or three months studying that part of the manuscript in great detail.
sentences.zh: 即使向数学家解释它也需要数学家花两三个月的时间来详细研究手稿的这一部分。

sentences.en: NOVA: Eventually, after a year of work, and after inviting the Cambridge mathematician Richard Taylor to work with you on the error, you managed to repair the proof.
sentences.zh: NOVA：最终，经过一年的工作，并邀请剑桥数学家理查德·泰勒与你一起解决这个错误，你成功地修复了证明。

sentences.en: The question that everybody asks is this; is your proof the same as Fermat's?
sentences.zh: 每个人都会问的问题是这样的；你的证明和费马的证明一样吗？

sentences.en: AW: There's no chance of that.
sentences.zh: 艾：没有这样的机会。

sentences.en: Fermat couldn't possibly have had this proof.
sentences.zh: 费马不可能有这个证明。

sentences.en: It's 150 pages long.
sentences.zh: 它有 150 页长。

sentences.en: It's a 20th-century proof.
sentences.zh: 这是20世纪的证据。

sentences.en: It couldn't have been done in the 19th century, let alone the 17th century.
sentences.zh: 这在 19 世纪是不可能做到的，更不用说在 17 世纪了。

sentences.en: The techniques used in this proof just weren't around in Fermat's time.
sentences.zh: 这个证明中使用的技术在费马时代还没有出现。

sentences.en: NOVA: So Fermat's original proof is still out there somewhere.
sentences.zh: NOVA：所以费马的原始证明仍然存在于某处。

sentences.en: AW: I don't believe Fermat had a proof.
sentences.zh: AW：我不相信费马有证明。

sentences.en: I think he fooled himself into thinking he had a proof.
sentences.zh: 我认为他自欺欺人地认为他有证据。

sentences.en: But what has made this problem special for amateurs is that there's a tiny possibility that there does exist an elegant 17th-century proof.
sentences.zh: 但这个问题对业余爱好者来说特别重要的是，确实存在 17 世纪优雅的证明的可能性很小。

sentences.en: NOVA: So some mathematicians might continue to look for the original proof.
sentences.zh: NOVA：所以一些数学家可能会继续寻找原始证明。

sentences.en: What will you do next?
sentences.zh: 接下来你会做什么？

sentences.en: AW: There's no problem that will mean the same to me.
sentences.zh: AW：没有任何问题对我来说具有同样的意义。

sentences.en: Fermat was my childhood passion.
sentences.zh: 费马是我儿时的爱好。

sentences.en: There's nothing to replace it.
sentences.zh: 没有什么可以替代它。

sentences.en: I'll try other problems.
sentences.zh: 我会尝试其他问题。

sentences.en: I'm sure that some of them will be very hard and I'll have a sense of achievement again, but nothing will mean the same to me.
sentences.zh: 我确信其中一些会非常困难，我会再次有成就感，但对我来说没有什么是一样的。

sentences.en: There's no other problem in mathematics that could hold me the way that this one did.
sentences.zh: 数学中没有其他问题可以像这道问题那样困扰我。

sentences.en: There is a sense of melancholy.
sentences.zh: 有一种惆怅的感觉。

sentences.en: We've lost something that's been with us for so long, and something that drew a lot of us into mathematics.
sentences.zh: 我们失去了一些陪伴我们很久的东西，以及一些吸引我们很多人进入数学的东西。

sentences.en: But perhaps that's always the way with math problems, and we just have to find new ones to capture our attention.
sentences.zh: 但也许数学问题总是这样，我们只需要找到新的问题来吸引我们的注意力即可。

sentences.en: People have told me I've taken away their problem—can't I give them something else?
sentences.zh: 人们告诉我，我已经解决了他们的问题——我不能给他们一些别的东西吗？

sentences.en: I feel some sense of responsibility.
sentences.zh: 我感到有些责任感。

sentences.en: I hope that seeing the excitement of solving this problem will make young mathematicians realize that there are lots and lots of other problems in mathematics which are going to be just as challenging in the future.
sentences.zh: 我希望看到解决这个问题的兴奋能让年轻的数学家意识到数学中还有很多很多其他问题在未来也同样具有挑战性。

sentences.en: NOVA: What is the main challenge now?
sentences.zh: NOVA：现在主要的挑战是什么？

sentences.en: AW: The greatest problem for mathematicians now is probably the Riemann Hypothesis.
sentences.zh: AW：现在数学家面临的最大问题可能是黎曼猜想。

sentences.en: But it's not a problem that can be simply stated.
sentences.zh: 但这不是一个可以简单说出来的问题。

sentences.en: NOVA: And is there any one particular thought that remains with you now that Fermat's Last Theorem has been laid to rest?
sentences.zh: NOVA：既然费马大定理已经被搁置了，你还有什么特别的想法吗？

sentences.en: AW: Certainly one thing that I've learned is that it is important to pick a problem based on how much you care about it.
sentences.zh: AW：当然，我学到的一件事是，根据你对问题的关心程度来选择问题很重要。

sentences.en: However impenetrable it seems, if you don't try it, then you can never do it.
sentences.zh: 不管看起来多么高深莫测，如果你不去尝试，那么你永远做不到。

sentences.en: Always try the problem that matters most to you.
sentences.zh: 始终尝试对您来说最重要的问题。

sentences.en: I had this rare privilege of being able to pursue in my adult life, what had been my childhood dream.
sentences.zh: 我有这种难得的荣幸，能够在成年生活中追求我儿时的梦想。

sentences.en: I know it's a rare privilege, but if one can really tackle something in adult life that means that much to you, then it's more rewarding than anything I can imagine.
sentences.zh: 我知道这是一种难得的特权，但如果一个人能够真正解决成年生活中对你来说意义重大的事情，那么这比我能想象的任何事情都更有意义。

sentences.en: NOVA: And now that journey is over, there must be a certain sadness?
sentences.zh: NOVA：现在旅程结束了，一定会有某种悲伤吧？

sentences.en: AW: There is a certain sense of sadness, but at the same time there is this tremendous sense of achievement.
sentences.zh: AW：有一定的悲伤感，但同时也有巨大的成就感。

sentences.en: There's also a sense of freedom.
sentences.zh: 还有一种自由感。

sentences.en: I was so obsessed by this problem that I was thinking about it all the time—when I woke up in the morning, when I went to sleep at night—and that went on for eight years.
sentences.zh: 我对这个问题非常着迷，以至于我一直在思考它——早上醒来时，晚上睡觉时——这样的情况持续了八年。

sentences.en: That's a long time to think about one thing.
sentences.zh: 思考一件事要花很长时间。

sentences.en: That particular odyssey is now over.
sentences.zh: 这段特别的冒险之旅现在结束了。

sentences.en: My mind is now at rest.
sentences.zh: 现在我的心已经平静了。

blocks.html_en:
Solving Fermat: Andrew Wiles

Andrew Wiles devoted much of his entire career to proving Fermat's Last Theorem, the world's most famous mathematical problem. In 1993, he made front-page headlines when he announced a proof of the problem, but this was not the end of the story; an error in his calculation jeopardized his life's work. Andrew Wiles spoke to NOVA and described how he came to terms with the mistake, and eventually went on to achieve his life's ambition.

NOVA: Many great scientific discoveries are the result of obsession, but in your case that obsession has held you since you were a child.

ANDREW WILES: I grew up in Cambridge in England, and my love of mathematics dates from those early childhood days. I loved doing problems in school. I'd take them home and make up new ones of my own. But the best problem I ever found, I found in my local public library. I was just browsing through the section of math books and I found this one book, which was all about one particular problem—Fermat's Last Theorem. This problem had been unsolved by mathematicians for 300 years. It looked so simple, and yet all the great mathematicians in history couldn't solve it. Here was a problem, that I, a ten year old, could understand and I knew from that moment that I would never let it go. I had to solve it.

blocks.html_en:
AW: Fermat was a 17th-century mathematician who wrote a note in the margin of his book stating a particular proposition and claiming to have proved it. His proposition was about an equation which is closely related to Pythagoras' equation. Pythagoras' equation gives you:
x2 + y2 = z2

You can ask, what are the whole number solutions to this equation, and you can see that:

32 + 42 = 52

and

52 + 122 = 132

And if you go on looking then you find more and more such solutions. Fermat then considered the cubed version of this equation:

x3 + y3 = z3

He raised the question: can you find solutions to the cubed equation? He claimed that there were none. In fact, he claimed that for the general family of equations:

xn + yn = zn where n is bigger than 2

it is impossible to find a solution. That's Fermat's Last Theorem.

NOVA: So Fermat said because he could not find any solutions to this equation, then there were no solutions?

blocks.html_en:
AW: He did more than that. Just because we can't find a solution it doesn't mean that there isn't one. Mathematicians aren't satisfied because they know there are no solutions up to four million or four billion, they really want to know that there are no solutions up to infinity. And to do that we need a proof. Fermat said he had a proof. Unfortunately, all he ever wrote down was: "I have a truly marvelous demonstration of this proposition which this margin is too narrow to contain."

NOVA: What do you mean by a proof?

AW: In a mathematical proof you have a line of reasoning consisting of many, many steps, that are almost self-evident. If the proof we write down is really rigorous, then nobody can ever prove it wrong. There are proofs that date back to the Greeks that are still valid today.

NOVA: So the challenge was to rediscover Fermat's proof of the Last Theorem. Why did it become so famous?

AW: Well, some mathematics problems look simple, and you try them for a year or so, and then you try them for a hundred years, and it turns out that they're extremely hard to solve. There's no reason why these problems shouldn't be easy, and yet they turn out to be extremely intricate. The Last Theorem is the most beautiful example of this.

NOVA: But finding a proof has no applications in the real world; it is a purely abstract question. So why have people put so much effort into finding a proof?

AW: Pure mathematicians just love to try unsolved problems—they love a challenge. And as time passed and no proof was found, it became a real challenge. I've read letters in the early 19th century which said that it was an embarrassment to mathematics that the Last Theorem had not been solved. And of course, it's very special because Fermat said that he had a proof.

blocks.html_en:
AW: In my early teens I tried to tackle the problem as I thought Fermat might have tried it. I reckoned that he wouldn't have known much more math than I knew as a teenager. Then when I reached college, I realized that many people had thought about the problem during the 18th and 19th centuries and so I studied those methods. But I still wasn't getting anywhere. Then when I became a researcher, I decided that I should put the problem aside. It's not that I forgot about it—it was always there—but I realized that the only techniques we had to tackle it had been around for 130 years. It didn't seem that these techniques were really getting to the root of the problem. The problem with working on Fermat was that you could spend years getting nowhere. It's fine to work on any problem, so long as it generates interesting mathematics along the way—even if you don't solve it at the end of the day. The definition of a good mathematical problem is the mathematics it generates rather than the problem itself.

NOVA: It seems that the Last Theorem was considered impossible, and that mathematicians could not risk wasting getting nowhere. But then in 1986 everything changed. A breakthrough by Ken Ribet at the University of California at Berkeley linked Fermat's Last Theorem to another unsolved problem, the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. Can you remember how you reacted to this news?

blocks.html_en:
AW: It was one evening at the end of the summer of 1986 when I was sipping iced tea at the house of a friend. Casually in the middle of a conversation this friend told me that Ken Ribet had proved a link between Taniyama-Shimura and Fermat's Last Theorem. I was electrified. I knew that moment that the course of my life was changing because this meant that to prove Fermat's Last Theorem all I had to do was to prove the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. It meant that my childhood dream was now a respectable thing to work on. I just knew that I could never let that go.

NOVA: So, because Taniyama-Shimura was a modern problem, this meant that working on it, and by implication trying to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, was respectable.

AW: Yes. Nobody had any idea how to approach Taniyama-Shimura but at least it was mainstream mathematics. I could try and prove results, which, even if they didn't get the whole thing, would be worthwhile mathematics. So the romance of Fermat, which had held me all my life, was now combined with a problem that was professionally acceptable.

NOVA: At this point you decided to work in complete isolation. You told nobody that you were embarking on a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Why was that?

AW: I realized that anything to do with Fermat's Last Theorem generates too much interest. You can't really focus yourself for years unless you have undivided concentration, which too many spectators would have destroyed.

NOVA: But presumably you told your wife what you were doing?

AW: My wife's only known me while I've been working on Fermat. I told her on our honeymoon, just a few days after we got married. My wife had heard of Fermat's Last Theorem, but at that time she had no idea of the romantic significance it had for mathematicians, that it had been such a thorn in our flesh for so many years.

blocks.html_en:
AW: I used to come up to my study, and start trying to find patterns. I tried doing calculations which explain some little piece of mathematics. I tried to fit it in with some previous broad conceptual understanding of some part of mathematics that would clarify the particular problem I was thinking about. Sometimes that would involve going and looking it up in a book to see how it's done there. Sometimes it was a question of modifying things a bit, doing a little extra calculation. And sometimes I realized that nothing that had ever been done before was any use at all. Then I just had to find something completely new; it's a mystery where that comes from. I carried this problem around in my head basically the whole time. I would wake up with it first thing in the morning, I would be thinking about it all day, and I would be thinking about it when I went to sleep. Without distraction, I would have the same thing going round and round in my mind. The only way I could relax was when I was with my children. Young children simply aren't interested in Fermat. They just want to hear a story and they're not going to let you do anything else.

NOVA: Usually people work in groups and use each other for support. What did you do when you hit a brick wall?

blocks.html_en:
AW: When I got stuck and I didn't know what to do next, I would go out for a walk. I'd often walk down by the lake. Walking has a very good effect in that you're in this state of relaxation, but at the same time you're allowing the sub-conscious to work on you. And often if you have one particular thing buzzing in your mind then you don't need anything to write with or any desk. I'd always have a pencil and paper ready and, if I really had an idea, I'd sit down at a bench and I'd start scribbling away.

NOVA: So for seven years you're pursuing this proof. Presumably there are periods of self-doubt mixed with the periods of success.

AW: Perhaps I can best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of a journey through a dark unexplored mansion. You enter the first room of the mansion and it's completely dark. You stumble around bumping into the furniture, but gradually you learn where each piece of furniture is. Finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch, you turn it on, and suddenly it's all illuminated. You can see exactly where you were. Then you move into the next room and spend another six months in the dark. So each of these breakthroughs, while sometimes they're momentary, sometimes over a period of a day or two, they are the culmination of—and couldn't exist without—the many months of stumbling around in the dark that proceed them.

NOVA: And during those seven years, you could never be sure of achieving a complete proof.

AW: I really believed that I was on the right track, but that did not mean that I would necessarily reach my goal. It could be that the methods needed to take the next step may simply be beyond present day mathematics. Perhaps the methods I needed to complete the proof would not be invented for a hundred years. So even if I was on the right track, I could be living in the wrong century.

NOVA: Then eventually in 1993, you made the crucial breakthrough.

blocks.html_en:
AW: Yes, it was one morning in late May. My wife, Nada, was out with the children and I was sitting at my desk thinking about the last stage of the proof. I was casually looking at a research paper and there was one sentence that just caught my attention. It mentioned a 19th-century construction, and I suddenly realized that I should be able to use that to complete the proof. I went on into the afternoon and I forgot to go down for lunch, and by about three or four o'clock, I was really convinced that this would solve the last remaining problem. It got to about tea time and I went downstairs and Nada was very surprised that I'd arrived so late. Then I told her I'd solved Fermat's Last Theorem.

NOVA: The New York Times exclaimed "At Last Shout of 'Eureka!' in Age-Old Math Mystery," but unknown to them, and to you, there was an error in your proof. What was the error?

AW: It was an error in a crucial part of the argument, but it was something so subtle that I'd missed it completely until that point. The error is so abstract that it can't really be described in simple terms. Even explaining it to a mathematician would require the mathematician to spend two or three months studying that part of the manuscript in great detail.

NOVA: Eventually, after a year of work, and after inviting the Cambridge mathematician Richard Taylor to work with you on the error, you managed to repair the proof. The question that everybody asks is this; is your proof the same as Fermat's?

AW: There's no chance of that. Fermat couldn't possibly have had this proof. It's 150 pages long. It's a 20th-century proof. It couldn't have been done in the 19th century, let alone the 17th century. The techniques used in this proof just weren't around in Fermat's time.

NOVA: So Fermat's original proof is still out there somewhere.

AW: I don't believe Fermat had a proof. I think he fooled himself into thinking he had a proof. But what has made this problem special for amateurs is that there's a tiny possibility that there does exist an elegant 17th-century proof.

NOVA: So some mathematicians might continue to look for the original proof. What will you do next?

content_html_zh: 解决费马：安德鲁·怀尔斯 安德鲁·怀尔斯将他整个职业生涯的大部分时间都投入到了证明费马大定理这一世界上最著名的数学问题上。 1993年，当他宣布了该问题的证明时，他登上了头版头条，但这并不是故事的结局；他的计算错误危及了他一生的工作。 安德鲁·怀尔斯 (Andrew Wiles) 接受了 NOVA 采访，描述了他如何接受这个错误，并最终实现他的人生抱负。 NOVA：许多伟大的科学发现都是痴迷的结果，但就你而言，这种痴迷从你还是个孩子的时候起就一直困扰着你。 ANDREW WILES：我在英国剑桥长大，我对数学的热爱可以追溯到童年时期。 我喜欢在学校做题。 我会把它们带回家，自己制作新的。 但我发现的最好的问题是在当地的公共图书馆找到的。 我刚刚浏览了数学书籍的部分，发现了这一本书，它全部都是关于一个特定的问题——费马大定理。 这个问题300年来一直没有被数学家解决。 看起来如此简单，然而历史上所有伟大的数学家都无法解决它。 这是一个我十岁的孩子能够理解的问题，从那一刻起我就知道我永远不会放手。 我必须解决它。 NOVA：费马是谁？他的大定理是什么？ AW：费马是一位 17 世纪的数学家，他在书的页边写下了一个注释，陈述了一个特定的命题，并声称已经证明了它。 他的命题是关于一个与毕达哥拉斯方程密切相关的方程。 毕达哥拉斯方程给出：x2 + y2 = z2 你可以问，这个方程的整数解是多少，你可以看到：32 + 42 = 52 和 52 + 122 = 132 如果你继续寻找，你会发现越来越多的这样的解。 费马随后考虑了这个方程的立方版本：x3 + y3 = z3 他提出了一个问题：你能找到立方方程的解吗？ 他声称没有。 事实上，他声称对于一般方程组：xn + yn = zn（其中 n 大于 2），不可能找到解。 这就是费马大定理。 NOVA：所以费马说因为他找不到这个方程的任何解，所以就没有解？ AW：他做的还不止这些。 仅仅因为我们找不到解决方案，并不意味着没有解决方案。 数学家们并不满意，因为他们知道没有达到四百万或四十亿的解，他们真的想知道没有达到无穷大的解。 为此，我们需要一个证明。 费马说他有证明。 不幸的是，他只写下了：“我对这个命题有一个真正精彩的论证，但这个空白太窄了，无法容纳。” NOVA：你所说的证明是什么意思？ AW：在数学证明中，你有一系列推理，其中包含许多很多步骤，这些步骤几乎是不言而喻的。 如果我们写下的证明真的很严格，那么没有人能证明它是错误的。 有一些可以追溯到希腊人的证据至今仍然有效。 NOVA：所以挑战是重新发现费马大定理的证明。 为什么它变得如此出名？ 艾：嗯，有些数学问题看起来很简单，你尝试了一年左右，然后尝试了一百年，结果发现它们非常难解决。 这些问题没有理由不容易解决，但事实证明它们极其复杂。 最后定理就是最好的例子。 NOVA：但是找到证明在现实世界中没有应用；这是一个纯粹抽象的问题。 那么为什么人们要花费如此多的精力来寻找证据呢？ AW：纯粹的数学家只是喜欢尝试未解决的问题——他们喜欢挑战。 随着时间的推移，没有找到证据，这成为一个真正的挑战。 我读过 19 世纪初的信件，信中说大定理尚未得到解决对数学来说是一个尴尬。 当然，这很特别，因为费马说他有证明。 NOVA：你是如何开始寻找证据的？ AW：在我十几岁的时候，我试图解决这个问题，因为我认为费马可能已经尝试过。 我估计他对数学的了解不会比我十几岁的时候多多少。 然后当我上大学时，我意识到很多人在18、19世纪就思考过这个问题，所以我研究了那些方法。 但我仍然一事无成。 当我成为一名研究员后，我决定把这个问题放在一边。 这并不是说我忘记了它——它一直都在那里——但我意识到我们解决这个问题的唯一技术已经存在了 130 年。 这些技术似乎并没有真正解决问题的根源。 研究费马的问题在于，你可能会花费数年时间一事无成。 解决任何问题都很好，只要它一路上产生有趣的数学——即使你最终没有解决它。 一个好的数学问题的定义是它产生的数学，而不是问题本身。 NOVA：似乎最后一个定理被认为是不可能的，数学家不能冒险浪费资源，一事无成。 但到了 1986 年，一切都发生了变化。 加州大学伯克利分校的肯·里贝特（Ken Ribet）取得的突破将费马大定理与另一个未解决的问题——谷山-志村猜想——联系起来。 你还记得你对这个消息的反应吗？ AW：那是1986年夏末的一个晚上，我在一位朋友家里喝着冰茶。 在一次谈话中，这位朋友偶然告诉我，肯·里贝特已经证明了谷山志村和费马大定理之间的联系。 我惊呆了。 那一刻我知道我的人生轨迹正在改变，因为这意味着要证明费马大定理，我所要做的就是证明谷山-志村猜想。 这意味着我儿时的梦想现在是一件值得尊敬的事情。 我只知道我永远不能放手。 NOVA：所以，因为谷山-志村问题是一个现代问题，这意味着研究它，并暗示试图证明费马大定理，是值得尊敬的。 艾伟：是的。 没有人知道如何研究谷山志村，但至少它是主流数学。 我可以尝试并证明结果，即使他们没有得到全部结果，这些结果也是有价值的数学。 因此，费马的浪漫一直困扰着我，现在却与一个在专业上可以接受的问题结合在一起。 NOVA：此时您决定完全隔离地工作。 你告诉任何人你正在着手证明费马大定理。 为什么会这样？ AW：我意识到任何与费马大定理有关的事情都会引起太多的兴趣。 除非你全神贯注，否则你不可能多年真正集中注意力，而太多的观众会破坏你的注意力。 NOVA：但想必你告诉了你的妻子你在做什么？ AW：我妻子是在我从事费马研究时才认识我的。 我在蜜月时告诉她的，就在我们结婚几天后。 我的妻子听说过费马大定理，但当时她并不知道它对数学家的浪漫意义，多年来它一直是我们的肉中刺。 NOVA：在日常工作中，你是如何构建你的证明的？ AW：我过去常常开始研究，并开始尝试寻找模式。 我尝试做一些计算来解释一些数学知识。 我试图将其与之前对数学某些部分的一些广泛的概念性理解相结合，以澄清我正在考虑的特定问题。 有时这需要去书本上查找，看看它是如何完成的。 有时这是一个稍微修改一些东西，做一些额外计算的问题。 有时我意识到以前做过的任何事情都没有任何用处。 然后我只需要找到一些全新的东西；它是从哪里来的还是个谜。 我基本上一直在脑子里萦绕着这个问题。 我早上醒来的第一件事就是想到它，我会整天想着它，当我睡觉时我也会想着它。 如果没有分心，同样的事情就会在我的脑海里转来转去。 我唯一能放松的方式就是和孩子们在一起。 小孩子对费马根本不感兴趣。 他们只是想听一个故事，不会让你做任何其他事情。 NOVA：通常人们会分组工作并互相支持。 当你撞到砖墙时你会做什么？ AW：当我遇到困难并且不知道下一步该做什么时，我会出去散步。 我经常在湖边散步。 散步有很好的效果，因为你可以处于这种放松的状态，但同时你也可以让潜意识对你起作用。 通常，如果您脑子里有一件特定的事情在嗡嗡作响，那么您就不需要任何可以用来写字的东西或任何桌子。 我总是准备好铅笔和纸，如果我真的有一个想法，我就会坐在长凳上，开始乱写乱画。 NOVA：所以七年来你一直在追求这个证明。 想必在成功的时期中也夹杂着自我怀疑的时期。 AW：也许我最能描述我做数学的经历，就是穿越一座未经探索的黑暗宅邸的旅程。 你进入宅邸的第一个房间，里面一片漆黑。 你跌跌撞撞地撞到了家具，但渐渐地你就知道了每件家具的位置。 最后，大约六个月后，你找到灯开关，打开它，突然间一切都亮了。 您可以准确地看到您所在的位置。 然后你搬进隔壁房间，在黑暗中又度过了六个月。 因此，每一项突破虽然有时是短暂的，有时是一两天的时间，但它们都是数月在黑暗中摸索的结果，而且如果没有这些突破，它们就不可能存在。 NOVA：在那七年里，你永远无法确定能否获得完整的证明。 AW：我确实相信自己走在正确的道路上，但这并不意味着我一定会达到目标。 采取下一步所需的方法可能根本超出了当今的数学范围。 也许我完成证明所需的方法一百年后都不会被发明出来。 因此，即使我走在正确的道路上，我也可能生活在错误的世纪。 NOVA：最终在 1993 年，你取得了关键的突破。 AW：是的，那是五月下旬的一个早晨。 我的妻子娜达（Nada）带着孩子们出去了，而我则坐在办公桌前思考证明的最后阶段。 我随意地看一篇研究论文，有一句话引起了我的注意。 它提到了一个19世纪的构造，我突​​然意识到我应该可以用它来完成证明。 一直持续到下午，我忘记了下去吃午饭，到了大约三四点的时候，我真的确信这将解决最后一个剩下的问题。 下午茶时间到了，我下了楼，纳达对我这么晚才到感到非常惊讶。 然后我告诉她我已经解决了费马大定理。 NOVA：《纽约时报》惊呼“‘尤里卡’的最后一声呐喊！” 在古老的数学之谜中”，但他们和你都不知道，你的证明中有一个错误。 错误是什么？ AW：这是论证的关键部分中的一个错误，但它是如此微妙，以至于我在那之前完全错过了它。 该错误非常抽象，无法用简单的术语来描述。 即使向数学家解释它也需要数学家花两三个月的时间来详细研究手稿的这一部分。 NOVA：最终，经过一年的工作，并邀请剑桥数学家理查德·泰勒与你一起解决这个错误，你成功地修复了证明。 每个人都会问的问题是这样的；你的证明和费马的证明一样吗？ 艾：没有这样的机会。 费马不可能有这个证明。 它有 150 页长。 这是20世纪的证据。 这在 19 世纪是不可能做到的，更不用说在 17 世纪了。 这个证明中使用的技术在费马时代还没有出现。 NOVA：所以费马的原始证明仍然存在于某处。 AW：我不相信费马有证明。 我认为他自欺欺人地认为他有证据。 但这个问题对业余爱好者来说特别重要的是，确实存在 17 世纪优雅的证明的可能性很小。 NOVA：所以一些数学家可能会继续寻找原始证明。 接下来你会做什么？ AW：没有任何问题对我来说具有同样的意义。 费马是我儿时的爱好。 没有什么可以替代它。 我会尝试其他问题。 我确信其中一些会非常困难，我会再次有成就感，但对我来说没有什么是一样的。 数学中没有其他问题可以像这道问题那样困扰我。 有一种惆怅的感觉。 我们失去了一些陪伴我们很久的东西，以及一些吸引我们很多人进入数学的东西。 但也许数学问题总是这样，我们只需要找到新的问题来吸引我们的注意力即可。 人们告诉我，我已经解决了他们的问题——我不能给他们一些别的东西吗？ 我感到有些责任感。 我希望看到解决这个问题的兴奋能让年轻的数学家意识到数学中还有很多很多其他问题在未来也同样具有挑战性。 NOVA：现在主要的挑战是什么？ AW：现在数学家面临的最大问题可能是黎曼猜想。 但这不是一个可以简单说出来的问题。 NOVA：既然费马大定理已经被搁置了，你还有什么特别的想法吗？ AW：当然，我学到的一件事是，根据你对问题的关心程度来选择问题很重要。 不管看起来多么高深莫测，如果你不去尝试，那么你永远做不到。 始终尝试对您来说最重要的问题。 我有这种难得的荣幸，能够在成年生活中追求我儿时的梦想。 我知道这是一种难得的特权，但如果一个人能够真正解决成年生活中对你来说意义重大的事情，那么这比我能想象的任何事情都更有意义。 NOVA：现在旅程结束了，一定会有某种悲伤吧？ AW：有一定的悲伤感，但同时也有巨大的成就感。 还有一种自由感。 我对这个问题非常着迷，以至于我一直在思考它——早上醒来时，晚上睡觉时——这样的情况持续了八年。 思考一件事要花很长时间。 这段特别的冒险之旅现在结束了。
